title: Security: WPA3 and Wi-Fi 7
summary: WPA3 closes WPA2’s weak points on shared-password (Personal) and staff sign-in (Enterprise) networks, and Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz require it for secured networks.

opener.promise: Stronger sign-in for shared-password and staff networks alike
opener.problem: A guessable WPA2 password can be cracked offline; devices can be fooled by fake access points.

wifi7Adds: WPA3 launched as its own certification in 2018 {{wpa3-launched}} and is now required for new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices {{wpa3-mandatory-cert}}. Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections require it {{wpa3-mlo-required}}, the 6 GHz band requires WPA3 and uses Enhanced Open for open access {{6ghz-security-options}}, and the WPA2-Enterprise sign-in is not used with Wi-Fi 7 or in 6 GHz {{wpa3-ent-6ghz-eht}}.

beats.heading: WPA2: two doors, two weak points

caption.headline: [[wpa2|WPA2]]: two doors, two weak points
caption.takeaway: A guessable shared password can be cracked offline; a [[fake-access-point|fake access point]] can fool devices.

beats.body:
Hospitals run two kinds of Wi-Fi sign-in through the same [[access-point|access points]]. Many clinical device networks use one shared password: [[wpa-personal|WPA2-Personal]]. Staff devices usually sign in with their own credentials: [[wpa-enterprise|WPA2-Enterprise]].

Each has a weak point. On the shared-password network, someone in the car park can record the moment a device joins, take the recording away and try millions of password guesses offline, unseen; a guessable password falls quickly {{wpa3-sae}}. On the staff network, WPA2 leaves checking the sign-in server’s certificate to each device’s configuration, which WPA3 makes mandatory {{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}, so a misconfigured device can be fooled by a [[fake-access-point|fake access point]]; and protecting control messages is optional {{wpa2-ent-pmf-optional}}.
beats.bottomLine: Both kinds of WPA2 network can be attacked quietly: one through a recorded sign-in, the other through a convincing fake.
beats.sceneDescription: A ward wall with two doors under an access point: a keypad door for the shared-password network, with an infusion pump in front, and a badge door for staff sign-in, with a workstation. An outsider copies a recorded sign-in from the keypad and carries it to a desk, where the lock pops open. At the staff door, the workstation is linked to a red fake access point instead of the real one.

callout.title: WPA2’s two weak points
points: Shared password: a recorded sign-in lets attackers guess offline{{wpa3-sae}}
Staff sign-in: certificate checks depend on device configuration{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}
Control messages can be forged when protection is left off{{wpa2-ent-pmf-optional}}

beats.heading: WPA3-Personal: nothing to take home

caption.headline: [[wpa3|WPA3]]-Personal: nothing to take home
caption.takeaway: A recording is useless for offline guessing; every guess must be tried live{{wpa3-sae}}.
caption.technical: [[sae|SAE]] replaces the shared-password handshake, and each session derives a unique key{{wpa3-forward-secrecy}}.

beats.body:
[[wpa3|WPA3]]-Personal replaces the shared-password handshake with [[sae|SAE]], an exchange designed so that a recording is useless for offline guessing: every guess requires talking to the real network {{wpa3-sae}}. WPA3 is required for new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices {{wpa3-mandatory-cert}}.

Each device also agrees a fresh key for every session, so if the password leaks later, traffic captured earlier stays protected: [[forward-secrecy|forward secrecy]] {{wpa3-forward-secrecy}}.
beats.bottomLine: WPA3 closes the most common way attackers break shared-passphrase networks, and it is already built into current devices.
beats.deepDive: SAE is a password-authenticated key exchange (the "dragonfly" handshake) followed by the standard 4-way handshake; each successful exchange yields a unique pairwise key {{wpa3-sae}}. WPA3 configurations require [[pmf|protected management frames (PMF)]], and WEP, TKIP and WPA version 1 are disallowed {{legacy-security-disallowed}}. Hash-to-element (H2E) derives the password element in constant time, closing side channels found in early SAE implementations {{wifi7-eht-security}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Back at the keypad door. The outsider’s recording turns into a sealed grey box that gives nothing to test, and their single live guess at the real keypad is refused. The infusion pump gets its own key for the session.

callout.title: What WPA3-Personal changes
points: A recorded sign-in gives nothing to test offline{{wpa3-sae}}
Every guess must be tried live, against the real network
Each session gets a fresh key, so leaks cannot unlock old traffic{{wpa3-forward-secrecy}}

questions.q: Why does forward secrecy matter if we rotate passwords?
questions.a: Rotation limits future exposure, but with WPA2-Personal a leaked passphrase can still decrypt traffic recorded earlier. WPA3-Personal derives a fresh key each session{{wpa3-forward-secrecy}}, so old recordings stay protected.

questions.q: What about guest Wi-Fi with no password?
questions.a: Wi-Fi Enhanced Open encrypts each guest device’s traffic without a password{{owe-what}}, so an open network is no longer readable by anyone nearby.

beats.heading: WPA3-Enterprise: no fooling the staff door

caption.headline: [[wpa3|WPA3]]-Enterprise: no fooling the staff door
caption.takeaway: Devices must check the server’s certificate{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}; Only mode also requires protected control messages{{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}}.
caption.technical: Only mode: SHA-256 sign-in replaces SHA-1{{wpa3-ent-sha256}}; Transition mode offers both{{wpa3-ent-transition}}.

beats.body:
On the staff network, [[wpa3|WPA3]]-Enterprise closes the fake-reader gap: a device signing in with EAP-TLS, EAP-TTLS or PEAP must validate the sign-in server’s [[server-certificate|certificate]] before trusting it {{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}, so a [[fake-access-point|fake access point]] cannot simply pose as the hospital.

WPA3-Enterprise has two modes. **Only mode** makes [[pmf|protected management frames]] mandatory {{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}}, so attackers cannot forge the control messages that knock devices off the network, and uses a stronger SHA-256 sign-in in place of SHA-1 {{wpa3-ent-sha256}}. **Transition mode** offers both sign-ins so WPA2- and WPA3-Enterprise devices can share one network during migration {{wpa3-ent-transition}}. Separately, a 192-bit mode serves the most sensitive networks {{wpa3-ent-192}}.
beats.bottomLine: Staff devices keep their credentials for the real network; in Only mode, a forged disconnect no longer works either.
beats.deepDive: In WPA3-Enterprise Only Mode the access point enables the 802.1X SHA-256 [[akm|AKM]] (00-0F-AC:5), disables the SHA-1 AKM and sets PMF Required {{wpa3-ent-sha256}} {{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}}. Server certificate validation is mandatory for EAP-TLS, EAP-TTLS and EAP-PEAP {{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}. The 192-bit mode uses only the Suite B 192-bit AKM with GCMP-256 and BIP-GMAC-256, and does not interoperate with other modes {{wpa3-ent-192}}.
beats.sceneDescription: At the staff door, the real badge reader shows a gold certificate seal, and the fake access point is gone because the device no longer trusts it. A shield above the link shows that control messages are protected, and the workstation gets its own key.

callout.title: What WPA3-Enterprise changes
points: Devices must check the sign-in server is genuine{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}
Only mode: protected control messages are mandatory{{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}}
Only mode: SHA-256 sign-in replaces SHA-1{{wpa3-ent-sha256}}
Transition mode lets WPA2 and WPA3 devices share a network{{wpa3-ent-transition}}

questions.q: We already use WPA2-Enterprise. What do we gain from WPA3?
questions.a: Mandatory certificate checks{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}, and in Only mode mandatory protected control messages{{wpa3-ent-pmf-required}} and SHA-256 sign-in{{wpa3-ent-sha256}}. Your sign-in server and credentials usually carry over; devices and access points need WPA3 support.

Only where policy demands the strongest suites. 192-bit mode uses its own sign-in and encryption suites and does not interoperate with other modes{{wpa3-ent-192}}, so every device on that network must support it.

Transition mode lets WPA2- and WPA3-Enterprise devices share one network on 2.4 and 5 GHz{{wpa3-ent-transition}}. Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz associations do not use the SHA-1 sign-in{{wpa3-ent-6ghz-eht}}, so plan Only mode there.

beats.heading: Required where it matters most

caption.headline: Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz: WPA3 sign-in
caption.takeaway: Both doors need WPA3 there{{wpa3-6ghz-required}}{{wpa3-ent-6ghz-eht}}; a separate older network is one migration option{{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}}.
caption.technical: Open guest networks in 6 GHz use Wi-Fi Enhanced Open instead{{6ghz-security-options}}.

beats.body:
With earlier Wi-Fi, WPA3 was optional and many networks stayed on WPA2. In the 6 GHz band and on Wi-Fi 7, that choice goes away for both kinds of network: WPA2-Personal is not permitted in 6 GHz {{wpa3-6ghz-required}}, Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections require WPA3 {{wpa3-mlo-required}}, and the WPA2-Enterprise sign-in is not used with Wi-Fi 7 or in 6 GHz {{wpa3-ent-6ghz-eht}}. Open guest networks there use Wi-Fi Enhanced Open {{6ghz-security-options}}.

Devices that cannot do WPA3 can keep working on a separate, older network while they are replaced, one migration option that Wi-Fi Alliance guidance describes {{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}}. On 2.4 and 5 GHz, transition modes are another {{wpa3-ent-transition}}.
beats.bottomLine: Moving to Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz is also a security upgrade: the strongest settings become the baseline rather than an option someone has to remember.
beats.deepDive: For networks with EHT enabled, the WPA3 deployment guide makes beacon protection mandatory in every mode; in WPA3-Personal Only mode it also marks as mandatory the SAE-GDH [[akm|AKM]] (suite 24), PMF required, SAE hash-to-element and both GCMP-256 and CCMP-128 pairwise ciphers {{wifi7-eht-security}}. A [[mld|multi-link device]] negotiates one security association that applies to all of its links {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. [[beacon-protection|Beacon protection]] lets devices detect forged beacons. These are deployment requirements, not certification rules, so confirm configuration options with each product.
beats.sceneDescription: Above both doors, the access point is labelled Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz, WPA3 sign-in. An older phone that supports only WPA2 is turned away from the main doors and moves to a smaller side door, a separate network for older devices, labelled as one migration option. A note shows what the earlier generation accepted.

callout.title: What changes on Wi-Fi 7
points: Shared-password networks in 6 GHz must use WPA3{{wpa3-6ghz-required}}
Staff networks on Wi-Fi 7 or 6 GHz use WPA3-Enterprise{{wpa3-ent-6ghz-eht}}
Older devices: a separate network is one migration option{{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}}

questions.q: Will our older clinical devices still connect?
questions.a: Devices without WPA3 cannot join 6 GHz networks{{wpa3-6ghz-required}} or Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections{{wpa3-mlo-required}}. Many long-lived clinical devices will stay on 2.4 and 5 GHz for years, on a separate network name{{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}} or a transition-mode network{{wpa3-ent-transition}}, until they are replaced.

beats.heading: Protecting clinical and device traffic

caption.headline: Protecting clinical and staff traffic
caption.takeaway: Every WPA3 device has its own key; benefits arrive as devices migrate.

beats.body:
Hospital networks carry clinical messages, device [[telemetry|telemetry]] and staff communications. Stronger sign-in and per-session encryption make it much harder to eavesdrop on or impersonate that traffic, on the devices that use WPA3.

WPA3 is one layer of security, not a complete programme: it complements network segmentation, device management and your organisation's security and compliance processes.
beats.bottomLine: Plan WPA3 alongside clinical device refresh: some older devices may not support it, so 6 GHz and Wi-Fi 7 networks may need separate network names during the transition.
beats.sceneDescription: Every device at both doors holds its own key, the outsider is gone, and the side door for older devices is marked to be retired as they are replaced.

callout.title: What to plan
points: List which clinical devices support WPA3
Move staff networks to WPA3-Enterprise with certificate checks on{{wpa3-ent-cert-validation}}
If older devices need one, a separate network with a retirement date{{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}}

questions.q: Does WPA3 make our network compliant?
questions.a: No single feature does. WPA3 is one layer of security; it complements network segmentation, device management and your organisation’s security and compliance processes.

keyFigures.note: Earlier generations have no multi-link operation.

lineage.lead: A separate Wi-Fi Alliance security program, not part of one generation.
